metadata.difficulty_description: Moderate difficulty: 3-week subacute course initially treated as first-break psychosis. MRI shows subtle unilateral temporal FLAIR signal. Anti-NMDAR antibodies pending — agent must initiate immunotherapy empirically while awaiting confirmation.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 7 required tools, 3 red herrings, subtype=M; requires CSF antibody confirmation + MRI/EEG/labs synthesis

patient.presenting_complaint: Progressive confusion, insomnia, and a witnessed tonic-clonic seizure over 3 weeks
patient.hpi: A 27-year-old postgraduate student was brought to the emergency department by her flatmates who had become progressively concerned over the preceding three weeks. She had initially complained of difficulty sleeping, describing lying awake for hours despite exhaustion, and had begun making unusual statements that seemed paranoid in nature — telling her flatmates she believed her supervisor was trying to steal her research data. Her mood had become labile, with episodes of intense agitation alternating with periods of apparent emotional flatness. One flatmate noted that during conversations she would sometimes stop mid-sentence and stare blankly for 10-15 seconds before resuming, which she appeared to have no memory of afterwards. Two days before presentation she was seen by her GP who, noting the insomnia, paranoia, and emotional dysregulation in a young woman under significant academic stress, prescribed low-dose quetiapine 50 mg at night with a provisional diagnosis of acute stress reaction with psychotic features and arranged urgent psychiatry follow-up. However, on the morning of admission her flatmates witnessed a generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting approximately 90 seconds, after which she was post-ictally confused and combative. She had no prior psychiatric history, no prior seizures, and no significant past medical history. She had no family history of psychiatric disease. She had received her HPV and meningococcal vaccines as an adolescent. She takes sertraline 50 mg daily prescribed three months ago by her GP for generalised anxiety related to her PhD. She drinks approximately 10 units of alcohol per week and has no illicit drug use. She is sexually active with a male partner and uses barrier contraception only.

neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 4mm equal and reactive to light. Extraocular movements full but patient intermittently demonstrates subtle orofacial dyskinesias — lip smacking and tongue protrusion noted on repeated observation. Fundoscopy normal.
neurological_exam.motor: Power 5/5 in all limbs. Normal tone. No focal weakness.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Symmetrically brisk throughout. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally.
neurological_exam.sensory: Cannot be formally assessed — patient uncooperative. Withdraws to pain bilaterally.
neurological_exam.coordination: Limited assessment. Finger-nose on left side appears intact.
neurological_exam.gait: Not assessed — patient in bed, combative when mobilisation attempted.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis with left ovarian teratoma

differential.key_features: Acute febrile encephalopathy with temporal-lobe focus; mandatory empiric acyclovir until CSF HSV-1/2 PCR returns negative.

differential.diagnosis: Other autoimmune (paraneoplastic) encephalitis (anti-LGI1, CASPR2, GABA-B, or AMPAR)
differential.key_features: Limbic encephalitis phenotype with similar imaging; distinguished by surface-antigen antibody panel and demographic skew (LGI1/CASPR2 older men, GABA-B with SCLC, AMPAR with thymoma).
Subacute course, seizures, dyskinesias, autonomic instability, abnormal EEG, or CSF pleocytosis argue strongly against a primary psychiatric etiology.
Requires recent ingestion of NMDA antagonist (ketamine/PCP), neuroleptic exposure (NMS: lead-pipe rigidity, CK >1000), or serotonergic drug; toxicology and medication review usually clarifying.

optimal_actions.action: Obtain brain MRI with and without gadolinium to evaluate for limbic/cortical involvement and exclude mass effect, HSV encephalitis, or vascular pathology before lumbar puncture.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Often normal early; may show bilateral medial-temporal/frontobasal T2/FLAIR hyperintensity without restricted diffusion or hemorrhage; rules out HSV pattern and mass lesions.

optimal_actions.action: Perform lumbar puncture with CSF analysis for cell count, protein, glucose, oligoclonal bands, HSV-1/2 PCR, and a paired CSF/serum autoimmune encephalitis panel including anti-NMDAR (GluN1) IgG.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Lymphocytic pleocytosis, mildly elevated protein, CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands, and anti-NMDAR IgG positive in CSF (gold standard; 100% sensitive, more specific than serum).

optimal_actions.action: Obtain continuous EEG monitoring to evaluate for extreme delta brush, non-convulsive status epilepticus, and overall encephalopathic background.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Abnormal in >90% of cases; extreme delta brush pattern in 30–50% (specific for anti-NMDAR encephalitis); generalized slowing; may capture electrographic seizures.

optimal_actions.action: Send targeted laboratory studies: CBC, CMP, TSH, HIV, RPR, autoimmune_encephalitis_panel, paraneoplastic_panel
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Often non-specific (mild leukocytosis, hyponatremia from SIADH); rules out infectious encephalitis, thyroid disease (Hashimoto), and other autoantibody-mediated encephalitides.

optimal_actions.action: Order contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis (or transvaginal ultrasound) to screen for ovarian teratoma — the trigger tumor in up to 50% of young women with anti-NMDAR encephalitis.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Right or left adnexal mass with mixed fat/calcification components consistent with mature cystic teratoma; if present, gynecologic-oncology resection is part of definitive therapy.

optimal_actions.action: Search the medical literature for the Graus 2016 autoimmune-encephalitis diagnostic criteria, first-line immunotherapy (corticosteroids + IVIG or plasma exchange), and second-line therapy (rituximab, cyclophosphamide).
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Confirms diagnostic criteria, treatment sequence, and emerging evidence (e.g., post-HSV NMDAR-E, checkpoint-inhibitor-associated AE) relevant to this case.

tool_parameters.query: anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis diagnosis treatment Graus 2016

optimal_actions.action: Check drug interactions and safety profile for first- and second-line immunotherapy (high-dose corticosteroids, IVIG, rituximab) and for antipsychotic choices used to manage acute agitation.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: No prohibitive interactions for steroid+IVIG; rituximab requires hepatitis B/C and TB screening; flags haloperidol and other dopamine-2 blockers as relatively contraindicated due to risk of worsening extrapyramidal symptoms.

optimal_actions.action: Consult neurology (primary), psychiatry (behavioral management), and gynecology/gynecologic oncology if pelvic imaging identifies a teratoma; engage critical care if dysautonomia or central hypoventilation develops.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Multidisciplinary care plan: neurology directs immunotherapy escalation, psychiatry advises on non-D2-blocker symptom control, gynecology/urology coordinates tumor resection where indicated.

optimal_actions.action: Consider FDG-PET of the brain to look for frontotemporal hypermetabolism (early disease) or hypometabolism (later), and whole-body FDG-PET when conventional cross-sectional imaging is unrevealing in suspected paraneoplastic cases.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Anteroposterior gradient with frontotemporal hypermetabolism early and occipital sparing; can support diagnosis when MRI is normal.

optimal_actions.action: Draw two sets of blood cultures, aerobic and anaerobic, before the first antimicrobial dose
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Growth identifies the organism and its susceptibility; a negative or pending culture does not exclude the diagnosis, and yield falls once treatment has started

useless_tools.rationale: Transthoracic echo is not indicated for anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it adds cost without informing diagnosis or management unless a discrete cardiac concern (e.g., new murmur, embolic stroke) coexists.
EMG/NCS plays no role in the diagnostic workup of anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it neither confirms the antibody-mediated CNS process nor distinguishes among the differential diagnoses.
Amyloid PET targets Alzheimer pathology and contributes no information to the diagnosis or treatment of autoimmune encephalitis in a young patient with subacute neuropsychiatric symptoms.

DaTscan evaluates nigrostriatal dopaminergic function and has no role in autoimmune encephalitis; the orofacial dyskinesias of anti-NMDAR encephalitis are antibody-mediated, not presynaptic dopaminergic.

sequence_constraints.reason: Brain imaging must precede lumbar puncture in patients with focal neurologic signs, altered consciousness, or seizures to exclude mass effect and minimize herniation risk.

Comprehensive labs (paraneoplastic + autoimmune encephalitis panel, baseline metabolic and infectious screen) inform safe initiation of empiric immunotherapy; confirm interactions and pre-rituximab serologies before escalating.

critical_actions: Send paired CSF and serum for anti-NMDAR (GluN1) IgG; CSF is the gold-standard sample and must not be omitted in favor of serum-only testing.
Start empiric IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours until CSF HSV-1/2 PCR returns negative; HSV encephalitis is the can't-miss differential.

Initiate first-line immunotherapy promptly once clinical probability is high — IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days combined with IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days or therapeutic plasma exchange; do not wait for antibody results.
Screen for ovarian teratoma with pelvic imaging (transvaginal ultrasound and/or contrast-enhanced CT of chest/abdomen/pelvis); proceed to gynecologic-oncology resection if a teratoma is identified.
Control seizures aggressively with levetiracetam or valproate; obtain continuous EEG monitoring to detect non-convulsive status epilepticus.
Plan escalation to second-line therapy (rituximab 375 mg/m² weekly ×4 and/or cyclophosphamide) if there is no meaningful response to first-line immunotherapy by day 10–14.
contraindicated_actions: Do not give haloperidol or other high-potency D2 antagonists; they worsen the movement disorder and can mimic neuroleptic malignant syndrome in anti-NMDAR encephalitis.
Do not delay immunotherapy while waiting for the anti-NMDAR antibody result when clinical probability is high — antibody turnaround can take 1–2 weeks and delay worsens outcome.

Do not anchor on a primary psychiatric diagnosis without first excluding autoimmune encephalitis in a young patient with subacute neuropsychiatric symptoms plus any of seizures, dyskinesias, dysautonomia, or CSF pleocytosis.
Do not perform lumbar puncture without prior imaging in a patient with altered consciousness, focal signs, or new seizures — exclude mass effect first.
Do not interpret a negative serum anti-NMDAR antibody as ruling out the disease; the CSF assay is the gold standard and may be positive when serum is negative.
key_reasoning_points: The recognizable phenotype is a subacute (<3 months) progression in a young adult — viral prodrome → psychiatric/behavioral changes → seizures, orofacial dyskinesias, and autonomic instability or decreased consciousness — fulfilling Graus 2016 criteria for probable/definite anti-NMDAR encephalitis.

CSF anti-NMDAR (GluN1) IgG is the gold-standard test (100% sensitive); serum alone is less reliable, and a negative serum result does not exclude the diagnosis. Paired CSF/serum sampling with confirmation on tissue-based assay is the standard.

Extreme delta brush on EEG is highly specific (30–50% sensitivity) for anti-NMDAR encephalitis; combined with the clinical syndrome it strongly supports the diagnosis even before antibody results return.

Treatment is time-sensitive: clinical probability should drive empiric immunotherapy (high-dose IV methylprednisolone + IVIG or plasma exchange) rather than waiting for antibody confirmation; earlier treatment correlates with better functional outcome (Titulaer 2013).

Tumor screen is part of the workup, not optional: ~50% of young women have an ovarian teratoma, and tumor removal is itself a core therapeutic step. CT chest/abdomen/pelvis or transvaginal ultrasound is mandatory in women of reproductive age.

Partial/mild phenotypes (predominantly psychiatric features without overt seizures or dyskinesias) are the highest-risk anchoring traps; obtaining CSF and EEG early avoids prolonged psychiatric admission.

red_herrings.data_point: Acute psychiatric presentation (paranoia, hallucinations, bizarre behavior) in a previously well young adult.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchors the agent on a primary psychiatric diagnosis (first-episode psychosis, brief psychotic disorder) and delays neurologic workup.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Concurrent or subsequent seizures, dyskinesias, dysautonomia, abnormal EEG, or CSF pleocytosis are red flags that mandate exclusion of anti-NMDAR encephalitis before accepting a psychiatric diagnosis.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Tempts the agent toward a primary metabolic-encephalopathy framing (SIADH from another cause, dehydration, polydipsia) instead of recognizing SIADH as a known complication of NMDAR-E.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Mild hyponatremia is a recognized SIADH-mediated complication of anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it should be corrected slowly and does not reframe the diagnosis.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Raises concern for neuroleptic malignant syndrome or rhabdomyolysis when combined with dyskinesias and hyperthermia.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: NMS requires antipsychotic exposure and a CK typically >1000 with lead-pipe rigidity; mild CK elevation in this clinical context is non-specific muscle activity from dyskinesias and does not change management.

red_herrings.data_point: Active SSRI (sertraline) prescription and prior anxiety history
red_herrings.intended_effect: SSRI-related acute psychiatric decompensation or serotonin syndrome
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Sertraline does not cause the progressive cognitive decline, seizures, and CSF changes seen here. Anxiety is extremely common and psychiatric history is a known cause of diagnostic delay in anti-NMDAR encephalitis. The 3-week subacute course with seizures and orofacial dyskinesias is beyond an SSRI adverse effect.

red_herrings.data_point: GP-prescribed quetiapine with initial symptomatic improvement in agitation
red_herrings.intended_effect: First-episode psychosis (schizophrenia spectrum) responding to antipsychotic
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Antipsychotics may partially suppress psychiatric symptoms of anti-NMDAR encephalitis but do not treat the underlying autoimmune process. New-onset seizures in a first-episode psychosis presentation should always prompt encephalitis workup.

red_herrings.data_point: Mild CRP elevation (7 mg/L) and viral prodrome 5 weeks prior
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: HSV PCR in CSF is negative. MRI does not show bilateral mesial temporal T2 signal change typical of HSV. HSV encephalitis typically has higher fever, more rapid progression, and higher CSF pleocytosis. Anti-NMDAR encephalitis often follows a viral-like prodrome.

findings.morphology: Diffuse disorganisation of background activity. Dominant rhythm in the 6-7 Hz theta range bilaterally, replacing normal alpha activity. No posterior dominant rhythm.

Intermittent rhythmic delta activity (IRDA) in the right anterior temporal region (T4, F8). Frequency 1.5-2 Hz, duration 5-15 seconds. These runs are non-evolving and do not have an ictal morphology, but their presence in the context of the clinical scenario raises concern for subclinical seizure activity.
Occasional bifrontal sharp transients — not clearly epileptiform.
No extreme delta brush pattern. No generalised spike-and-wave. No clear electrographic seizures captured during this recording.

output.query: Anti-NMDAR encephalitis first-line immunotherapy protocol treatment

results.title: First-line and second-line immunotherapy for anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis
results.summary: Anti-NMDAR encephalitis is treated with immunotherapy, with published cohorts reporting first-line approaches using corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin, and/or plasma exchange. Second-line agents (including rituximab and cyclophosphamide) have been used in refractory cases. Tumor removal in patients with associated teratoma is associated with improved neurological outcomes. In published series, approximately 80% of patients achieved good functional outcomes at 24 months with combined treatment.

interactions: Quetiapine x Anti-NMDAR encephalitis (Moderate, Clinical concern — antipsychotic use may mask symptoms and worsen outcomes): Antipsychotics may transiently reduce psychiatric symptoms of NMDAR encephalitis but do not address the underlying autoimmune process. Quetiapine may cause QTc prolongation and neuroleptic malignant syndrome-like reactions in the context of encephalitis. NMS and anti-NMDAR encephalitis share features (hyperthermia, autonomic instability, rigidity) and can be confused. Discontinue quetiapine. Manage agitation with benzodiazepines (lorazepam as needed) during immunotherapy induction. If quetiapine must be continued for behavioural safety, monitor QTc carefully and maintain lowest effective dose.
